name: Espresso machine
description: Hot water under pressure passes through a firmly tamped bed of ground coffee, producing a concentrated drink in a short time.
steps: Grind the beans finely and measure the dose.
Distribute the ground coffee evenly in the portafilter and tamp it.
Lock the portafilter into the group head and start the shot.
Stop the shot once you have the desired volume. Serve immediately.

name: Pour-over (V60)
description: Pour-over is a manual brewing method in which hot water is slowly poured over ground coffee in a dripper lined with a paper filter. It produces a clean-tasting cup that brings out individual flavor notes.
steps: Place the filter in the dripper, rinse it with hot water, and discard the rinse water.
Add the ground coffee to the dripper and level the bed.
Wet the coffee with a small amount of water and wait 30–45 seconds.
Slowly pour in the remaining water in circular motions, in several stages.
Wait for the water to drain through the coffee, then serve.

name: French press
description: An immersion brewing method: ground coffee steeps in hot water in a carafe, then a plunger with a mesh filter separates the grounds. The result is rich and full-bodied.
steps: Grind the coffee coarsely and add it to the carafe.
Pour hot water over the coffee, making sure all the grounds are wet.
Cover with the lid without pressing the plunger and steep for about 4 minutes.
Slowly press the plunger down.
Pour the coffee into cups immediately to prevent further extraction.

name: AeroPress
description: A compact brewer in which coffee steeps in water and is then pressed through a filter with a plunger. Brewing parameters depend largely on the recipe, so only general steps are provided here.
steps: Insert the filter into the cap and rinse it with hot water.
Add the ground coffee to the chamber.
Pour in the water and stir.
Insert the plunger into the chamber and wait for the steeping time specified in your recipe.
Slowly press the plunger until you hear a characteristic hiss.

name: Moka pot
description: A stovetop brewer in which pressure from heated water pushes it up through ground coffee into the upper chamber. The result is strong and concentrated, but it is not espresso because the pressure is much lower.
steps: Fill the bottom chamber with water up to the safety valve.
Fill the filter basket with ground coffee and level it without tamping.
Screw the upper chamber on tightly.
Place the moka pot over low or medium heat with the lid open.
When the upper chamber is full and the flow starts sputtering, remove the pot from the stove.

name: Cezve (ibrik)
description: A traditional brewing method in which very finely ground coffee is heated with water in a small, long-handled metal pot. The coffee is served unfiltered, so the grounds settle at the bottom of the cup.
steps: Grind the coffee to a very fine consistency.
Pour cold water into the cezve, add the coffee and sugar to taste, then stir.
Place the cezve over low heat and do not let the mixture boil.
When foam begins to rise to the surface, remove the cezve from the heat.
Let the grounds settle briefly, then carefully pour the coffee into cups.

name: Cold brew
description: A brewing method in which coarsely ground coffee steeps in cold water for many hours. The result is usually smooth and refreshing, and it is often prepared as a concentrate.
steps: Grind the coffee coarsely.
Combine the ground coffee and cold water in a container.
Cover the container and leave it in the refrigerator for about 12–18 hours.
Strain through a paper filter or a fine-mesh sieve.
Dilute the concentrate with water or milk and serve over ice.
